steps.text: Part 3 of 4: The queen in a busy position. This part covers Using her lines; Her lines and your king. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

The queen is worth the most of any piece but the king: about nine pawns on the counting scale (a rule of thumb, not a law). So usually she should not take a pawn that a pawn can take back, unless the capture mates or wins more than the queen. [I] Before every capture ask one question: **does anything of theirs guard that square?**

steps.caption: The black knight on d6 is loose: nothing of Black's guards it. The queen sees it straight up the open file.

line.say: She takes the knight and nothing can take her back.
Black's king steps aside, a knight down.

steps.caption: The same slide, but now a pawn on c6 guards the pawn on d5. Taking it would cost the queen.

line.say: The queen takes a pawn along the open file.
But the pawn on c6 guards that square and takes her: nine points lost for one.

steps.caption: The pawn on e5 attacks the queen, and a pawn on d6 guards that pawn. Taking it would lose her, so she steps to a square no black piece attacks.

line.say: She moves along the file to d3, out of the pawn's reach.
Black's king steps aside; the queen is safe.

steps.caption: The black knight on b5 attacks the queen, but she cannot attack it: b5 is not on any of her lines. Knights attack by jumping.

line.say: She slips away along the file, to a square the knight does not attack.

claims.statement: A knight's square is not on her lines.

steps.text: [H] A guess, not a measured fact: when the queen comes out early, every piece that attacks her gains a free move, because she has to run. Test it: in the pawn-attack line below, count the moves each side made. The next three boards show one famous example.

steps.caption: White brings the queen out on move two, aiming along a diagonal at f7. [I] f7 is guarded only by the king at the start, which is why beginners often aim here. A bishop will help.

line.say: The queen glides up the diagonal to h5, in sight of the pawn on f7.
Black develops a knight and does not defend f7.
The bishop also aims at f7: now two white pieces attack it.

steps.caption: Black develops a knight, but it blocks nothing and leaves f7 guarded only by the king.

line.say: The queen takes on f7, guarded by the bishop, and it is checkmate.

steps.caption: Black has a better answer: a pawn move that attacks the queen. A pawn is worth one point and the queen nine, so she must run.

line.say: The pawn attacks the queen, and it also closes her diagonal.
The queen retreats. White has used two queen moves, while Black made useful moves with a pawn and a knight. [H] Early queen moves can cost tempi.

steps.text: The lesson of the three boards, and a rule of thumb: the queen is at her best once other pieces help her and few enemy pieces can hit her. [I] My inference from these boards: develop other pieces first, so the queen is not the first piece attacked. Judge each early queen move by one question: who can attack her next?

steps.caption: Here White's king is in check from the rook on e8. A queen move now has one job: end the check. Three squares do it.

line.say: She takes the rook that gives check, along the diagonal.
Her capture also gives check, so Black's king must move.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen can move to.

steps.caption: Her lines can also end the game. The black king is boxed in by its own pawns, and the d-file is open.

line.say: One long slide to the last rank: check, and no flight square, so it is checkmate.
